item.passage:
Ruth Abara had kept the scorebook for exactly one game before the Saturday it mattered, and that game had been a practice. Mr. Ochoa, who usually kept the book for the Eastside Hornets, had gone to his daughter's wedding in Tucson, and he had left Ruth his pencil, his eraser, and a page of instructions written in square capitals.

The instructions were mostly numbers. Every position on the field had one: the pitcher was 1, the catcher 2, and so on around the bases to the shortstop at 6 and the outfielders at 7, 8, and 9. A ground ball to the shortstop, who threw to first, went into the book as 6-3. A strikeout was a K. If the batter watched the third strike go by without swinging, the K was written backward. At the bottom of the page Mr. Ochoa had added one more line and underlined it twice: KEEP THE PITCH COUNT. THE HOME BOOK IS THE ONE THAT COUNTS.

So beside the batting lines Ruth kept a second column for her brother Danny, who was pitching, and every time he threw she made a mark. She made them in bundles of five, four straight strokes and a fifth across them, the way her grandmother kept score at cards.

Assistant Coach Lyle kept a count too, on a silver clicker he wore around his neck. In the fourth inning a foul ball struck a Hornets substitute in the elbow as he stood at the dugout fence, and Mr. Lyle ran to the snack bar for ice. The clicker went with him, bouncing on its cord. Danny threw four pitches while he was gone, and Ruth marked all four.

By the top of the sixth inning the Hornets led 3-2, and Danny was throwing harder than he had all spring. The league allowed a pitcher his age seventy-five pitches in a game. When the inning's second out was made, Coach Pruitt leaned over the bleacher rail and asked Ruth for her number.

"Seventy-five," she said.

Mr. Lyle held up his clicker. "Seventy-one."

Coach Pruitt looked from one to the other. Danny, on the mound, had heard both numbers and was looking at Ruth as if she had taken something from his pocket.

Ruth turned the book around so the coach could see it. He ran his finger down the column, counting the bundles under his breath, and she told him about the four pitches during the ice. Mr. Lyle looked down at his clicker for a long moment and then said, quietly, that she was right; he had carried it to the snack bar.

Danny came out of the game. He walked to the dugout without looking at the bleachers and dropped his glove on the bench hard enough that it slid off the far end. A boy named Theo got the third out on a ground ball, 6-3, the Hornets won 3-2, and Ruth wrote it down.

That night Danny knocked on her door. He had the scorebook, which she had left on the kitchen table, and he wanted to know which mark was the seventy-fifth. She found it for him, a short stroke slanted across four others, and he looked at it for a while and then asked her to show him how the backward K worked.

Behind the tire shop the city's runoff
slides through a concrete channel the width of a road,
and every morning on my way to the bus
the heron is there, up to its knees in it,

gray as the channel, gray as the morning,
so still that the first week I took it
for something a person had left: a coat rack,
a bent umbrella someone had set upright.

It holds one foot lifted for whole minutes.
It leans its long neck out over the water
the way my grandfather leaned over the sports page,
reading slowly, with his whole face.

Trucks go by on Ninth Street. A shopping cart
rusts on its side in the shallow end.
The water carries foam and a plastic lid,
and the heron lets all of it pass, waiting

for the one thing it came for, which I have seen
only twice: the neck unfolding faster than I can follow,
a silver flick, a swallow traveling down
the throat like a coin dropped into a sleeve.

I used to think a bird like that belonged
in a marsh on a calendar, among cattails,
lit gold at the edge of evening. I thought
a place like this was where wild things ended up.

Now I check for it the way you check
the sky before you leave the house.
On mornings it is gone the channel looks
like what it is, a ditch, and I walk faster.

On mornings it is there I miss the bus
on purpose, once or twice, and stand
at the chain-link fence with the trucks going by,
learning what it knows about a place to stand.

item.passage:
The summer I was fifteen I worked at the Bright Wave Car Wash on Route 9. It was a long tunnel of spinning cloth and soap jets with a crew of teenagers at each end. At the entrance we sprayed the wheels with a pink soap that smelled like bubble gum and steered each driver onto the track. At the exit we dried whatever the blowers had missed, which was most of it, with towels that came out of the dryer in the back still warm.

Mr. Castellano, the owner, had one rule, and he repeated it so often that we did impressions of him in the break room: Every car leaves dry. He meant every car, including the ones that came through in a drizzle, which seemed to me the purest waste of effort in the world. I said so once, to my friend Dani, while we toweled the hood of a minivan in the rain. Mr. Castellano heard me from the office door.

He did not argue. He walked over, took my towel, and handed me the minivan's keys, which the driver had left with us while she bought coffee across the road. "Open the door," he said.

I opened it, and a line of water ran off the top of the door frame and straight down the inside of my sleeve. The handle was wet too, and so was the little ledge of the frame where a driver rests a hand to climb in. I had dried the hood and the windshield, the parts you can see from across a parking lot. I had never once dried a handle.

item.prompt: Which of the following best summarizes the author's argument?
choices: Forecasters often raise the chance of rain to protect themselves from public blame.
The rain percentage is exact and reliable, and people need only learn what it measures.
The rain percentage should give way to plain words that every listener understands.
A forty percent chance means rain over forty percent of the area during the day.
Rain forecasts have improved because the government now keeps more careful records.
item.passage:
Few numbers are read as often, or as loosely, as the chance of rain. A morning forecast says forty percent, and one listener takes it to mean that rain will fall for forty percent of the day. Another pictures forty percent of the town getting wet while the rest stays dry. A third simply hears "probably not" and leaves the umbrella at home. All three are using the number, and each is using it to mean something other than what it says.

In the United States, the National Weather Service gives the number a narrow definition. A forty percent chance of rain means that, at any particular spot in the forecast area, there is a forty percent chance that at least a hundredth of an inch of rain will fall during the forecast period. It says nothing about how long the rain will last or how hard it will come down. A forecast of forty percent could describe a day with a scattered shower or two somewhere in the county, or a day when forecasters are quite sure that rain will fall but expect it to cover only part of the area.

It is tempting to blame the forecasters for the confusion, and some writers have suggested dropping the percentage altogether in favor of words like "likely" and "possible." I think that would be a mistake. Words are slipperier than numbers. Ask ten people what "likely" means and you will get answers ranging from a little better than even to nearly certain. The number, at least, means the same thing to everyone who has learned its definition.

There is also good reason to trust it. When records of government forecasts are checked against what actually happened, the two have generally been found to match well: of all the days given a thirty percent chance, rain has fallen on roughly three in ten. That is about as much as anyone can ask of a forecast. A thirty percent day that stays dry is still the forecast doing its job, since seven days in ten like it are supposed to stay dry.

What would help is a single sentence rather than a new number, taught once, perhaps in a middle school science class: the percentage is the chance that rain will reach the spot where you are standing. The number promises nothing more. A person who knows that sentence can decide for herself whether forty percent is worth carrying an umbrella for, which is the decision the forecast was meant to inform in the first place.

item.passage:
In the autumn of 1897 the children of Tessaly Township went to school in seven buildings, each with one room, one stove, and one teacher. The buildings stood about two miles apart, so that no child had to walk much farther than a mile, and each was attended by anywhere from nine to thirty pupils. The smallest, the Hollins school on the north road, had a teacher who was eighteen years old and had finished school herself only the spring before.

That winter the township board proposed something new. It would close four of the seven schools and carry their pupils by wagon to a larger building at Tessaly Crossing, where the older children could be taught in one room and the younger ones in another, each by a teacher who had taught at least five years. The wagons would be paid for out of the money saved on four teachers' salaries, four stoves, and four winters of coal.

The proposal was argued at three meetings in the Grange hall. Farmers asked what a wagon would cost. Mothers asked who would drive it, and what would happen to a six-year-old on an open wagon in a January wind. One man, Amos Reddick, said that he had walked a mile to school and his children could do the same, and that a township which carried its children would soon be expected to carry everything else.

The board answered the questions one at a time. The drivers would be chosen by sealed bid, but no bid would be accepted from a man under twenty-five. Each wagon would have canvas sides that could be let down in bad weather, and a row of bricks heated in the driver's kitchen stove would be laid along the floor for the children's feet. A driver who arrived late more than twice in a month would lose the route.

The wagons began running in September of 1898, three of them, each pulled by two horses along a route of about seven miles. By the end of the school year the board had a number to show for them. In the last year of the seven schools, the average pupil in the four closed districts had attended about half of the days school was in session. In the first year of the wagons, the same children attended about four days in five. The board's report gave the reason in one sentence: a child who is collected at the gate is a child who arrives.

The Reddick children walked to the Crossing that first year, a little over two miles each way, while the wagon from the north road passed them twice a day. In October of 1899 Amos Reddick appeared at the board's meeting and asked, without explaining himself, that the north wagon stop at his gate.

Most substances shrink as they cool, and most are denser as solids than as liquids. A lump of solid wax dropped into a pot of melted wax sinks to the bottom. Water breaks this rule twice, and the two exceptions together decide whether a lake in a cold climate can hold living things through the winter.

The first exception is the familiar one. Ice floats. When water freezes, its molecules lock into a regular, open framework, held in place by weak attractions called hydrogen bonds, and the framework takes up more room than the same molecules did when they were tumbling past one another as a liquid. The second exception is less familiar. As liquid water cools, it does grow denser, like other liquids, but only until it reaches about 4 degrees Celsius, a little above its freezing point.
